p:
So I would— so the beauty of the Parks Inspection program is that, uh, it is essentially the- the inspections are essentially randomized. So, and that, that can happen. So it

can work in either direction. The inspection can theoretically happen right before a big event or at the end, at the beginning of like a busy weekend, or it can happen at the end of a busy weekend. So it is a snapshot in time that, you know, so over you know, statistically, it will sort of account for, you know, what we're looking for is sort of a consistent level of service being provided to a park, even though at any given moment it could be really, really busy. And then, you know, so obviously when you walk through a park, you will experience it at that moment in time. So as these— excuse me— as these inspections are repeated over time, you're building sort of a statistical base where you can zoom out and sort of provide, you know, that way you can kind of rely on the data. Otherwise you're just getting captured in one specific moment in time.
So if it—

Oh, sorry, I just wanted to add to that because I think, uh, the— your question is a little bit about also how a specific event, how that's seen by our local park staff. So I think there's good— like, as part of that, um, special

event permit application and approval, there's the, the special event application goes to our special event permit staff for review. Part of their review is talking to the local park management about this event, the timing of the event. They get the approval of the local park staff. So the local park staff is then also gonna know when that event is happening. So, uh, they make sure that the site is ready for the event in the morning of the event. And our protocol is to try to have somebody from park maintenance kind of onsite checking that event, uh, especially at the end of the event to notice if they're, you know, 'cause, we require folks to clean up after their event. So if the event wasn't cleaned up after, if we— it's gonna require resources of, of ours. We note that to try to let that group know, like, you're, you're in violation or you didn't clean up appropriately, or we may have to charge you for that cleanup.

I was gonna ask, what, if any, enforcement measures are taken if you realize that a group did not, uh, you know, uphold their end

of the bargain and, and just to use that terminology, um, in terms of cleaning?

Yeah, I think that, you know, we- we try to work with groups, um, around making sure they understand the expectations and that they meet those expectations. If they haven't met those expectations, you know, we'll let them know. Um, we might just make sure in the next, um, the next time they apply for a permit, we- we do sometimes take bonds and those bonds are to help pay for things that- that they, you know, like any sort of damage or any additional cleanup and that's the purpose of the bond system.

Okay, thank you for that. Uh, because I am doing this hearing just a little differently, I want to make it more conversational, so I'm going to turn it to my colleague Council Member Morano, and then I'll jump back in.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you for your testimony today. And, uh, I also want to join Council Member Narcisse in, uh, praising the work of great groups like, uh, NYC H2O, which helped to make the, uh, parks in our district a lot cleaner and a lot better. So, thank you for your work. Uh,

by the way, for a group like NYC H2O, uh, I've heard some concern about how formalized the structure is for them to become a CBO. Can you speak briefly about how that actually occurs?

So I think we have, um, I think we have a good working relationship with the H2O. I think they do a lot of different programming, um, throughout our park system. I think most of that is taking place using special event permits. I think we're also in the- in the process of talking to them about using work permits because some of the work they're doing is actual restoration work and maybe would require a different kind of permit. Um, so again, not every, not every group, um, and especially H2O, which is, is lightly touching a lot of different areas, is, is, is the appropriate vehicle for, say, a license agreement, as I understand. But we can look more into— kind of, I'm not familiar specifically with all the complexity of that specific group, but happy to talk more as a follow up.

Thank you. Um, you mentioned in your testimony prioritizing historically underserved communities and equitable investment. Staten Island has more parkland per capita than any,

uh, any other borough. Can you tell me specifically how Staten Island fares in PFP staffing, grant funding, volunteer programming, and community partnership resources compared to the other boroughs?

Um, I, I mean, I, I'll just say top line, I think we look to distribute our resources equally— across the boroughs. Um, so we do have community engagement coordinators in Staten Island like we have in other boroughs. I think in terms of the money that we're giving out, it really is a function of who's applying for the money. I, I was excited to hear that in terms of the Catalyst program where we're actually, um, you know, reaching out to, to figure out parks that need more of that support and more organized volunteer groups. We are working with several Staten Island Parks and, and working to— with the Catalyst program to do specific outreach in Staten Island, which I'm excited about. And Heather, I'm going to turn it over to Heather who wants— if she wants to speak more to that.

Uh, yes. So we have a Catalyst organizer who is working along the North Shore Esplanade in Corporal Thompson Park and in Tappen Park. Um, and that's specifically to do community

engagement work at a very local level, and it's just those 3 parks that he's working in. So, I mean, the Esplanade is large, but it's just those 3 locations. Uh, in addition, we have been trying very hard to get as many groups as possible to apply for the Green Fund grant. Um, we've seen a slight increase. If you could get the word out to groups, we'd be happy to fund them.
Sure.
So, um, you know, we've, we've seen a slight increase as we try, you know, to get the word out, but any help that you could provide, we would love.

Uh, I was really glad to hear in, um, your testimony, Deputy Mayor, that the, the admission that the permitting system can be difficult to navigate, because it's been a frustration from a lot of the folks that, that I've heard from. I— in your testimony, you say that community organizations told you the special event permitting process was difficult to navigate. W— what specifically were the biggest complaints that you heard?

So as I said in the testimony, we did a series of 9 borough in-person forums last year where we invited, uh, groups to come and talk to us so they could both hear about what the special event permit process is and what the rules and requirements are, and also hear from them kind of what their challenges were and how we might be able to address them. So I think we have to - we have to keep in mind that we have a special event permit process in order to make sure that events that are happening in our parks are happening safely with the right, you know, not impinging on other people's use of, of the space, that, um, and a variety of other things that we have to keep in mind, right? So there's a lot of checks and balances here, uh, that we have to make sure we're providing for the safety of parkgoers. So we ask people to apply for-for— to host a special event using our special event, uh, process where we need people to apply at least 21 days in advance, but ideally months in advance. And sometimes things that people wanna do might require insurance. They might require— you have to go to NYPD for amplified sound permit. You might— if you

have a generator, you have to go to FDNY. And sometimes all of those requirements aren't necessarily clear to a small group up front. And so as they're trying to figure out their event, they're running into these obstacles. So I think, first of all, trying to provide more clarity up front, uh, where we've revised our website to make it more clear what some of those requirements are, um, is one of the things that, that, uh, we're doing. The other thing is we're putting together a pamphlet, again, just with this information on how to do a special event, trying to get our, uh, our rules and our requirements more out there so that they're familiar with it. I would say that, um, you know, PFP— one of the great things about PFP is that those community engagement coordinators can really hold the hands of small groups who may not understand the special event permits process and really help walk them through, help them develop that relationship with the special events, uh, borough permit coordinators, um, and make sure they're getting answers, you know, to their questions. The other thing we heard is that, you know, a bit of transparency. Like, they might be applying for a

site and that site might not be available and they wanna know, well, tell— how do I find out what site would be available? And so one of the things we did with our athletic permit process a few years ago is that we really were able to create more transparency by putting online a map of all our courts and fields and being able to show the public when those courts and fields are already permitted, so you're not applying for a permit for a site that's not available. So again, in some of our parks, there's a lot of demand. You might apply to do an event and that site's already taken. And so that's something we're looking to see if we can replicate with the special event permits process too, but that's still to come.

Chair, one final question, if I may? Um, I noticed a lot of impressive-sounding volunteer numbers in the testimony and briefing materials, but the Mayor's Management Report shows volunteer turnout declining. Can you explain that contradiction? Uh, er, are people counted multiple times? What exactly counts as a volunteer? Did the counting methodology change?

I think we have various ways we count volunteers, so my guess is gonna be like whatever is reported in the Mayor's Management Report might be a subset. Um, but I don't have that in front of me, so it's something we can get back to you. But, uh, Assistant Commissioner Smith, go ahead.

That's exactly what I was going to say. So, um, the Mayor's Management Report is exactly a subset of volunteerism, um, in the Parks Department. And, and as, uh, Commissioner Nelson said, volunteerism comes into parks in a variety of ways. In many different buckets. Um, so that is probably what's accounting for that discrepancy, um, in the report.
Yep.
Thank you.
Yep.
Uh, I believe that the Council Member gave you a promotion to Deputy Mayor, so congratulations.
I almost called you Mayor today. It's my third hearing of the day.

So I do have a couple follow-up questions before we go to the Bronx. Um, when will— so you mentioned a pamphlet that would, would help folks. Uh, when will that pamphlet be complete and ready for distribution?

It's— thank you for the question, Council Member. Um, it is in production at the moment. We are vetting a few final items. We're hoping to have it ready by the end of the year, and when we do produce it, it's going to be in multiple languages so that um, it's, it's accessible by, by all communities.

Thank you. Uh, does PFP work with local Council Member offices to get the word out about all the help that's out there? I, I, so I know that the resources are there, the help is there, but how do folks actually gain access to the help?

Yeah, I think we would love— we do work with Council Members' offices and we would love to work more with any Council Member that's interested. I mean, we can set— we can put together, like, an informational event. Um, we- we can attend any meetings you have with community members to kind

of, you know, promote our services. And I think, again, if you know of a group that's interested in volunteering in our park or doing some service in our park, you know, you should contact PFP and put them in touch because our community engagement coordinators can start that intake process of, like, talking to them about what they want to do, connect them to trainings, connect them to resources. So we want to be a resource for you and your community groups to engage with parks. Absolutely.
I'd love to— and we can talk about this offline— but I'd love to host, uh, a workshop here at 250 for members' offices.
We would love that. We would love that.
Before the summer gets here. Yep.
Yeah.
Thank you. Uh, one final question. This is for Heather. Can you name the neighborhoods that are currently benefiting from Green Fund grants?

Oh, uh, actually, I mean, Green Fund grants are pretty much all over the entire city,

but I will say I think it's 80% are focused in environmental justice communities. But basically we try to hit every neighborhood. So, uh, I mean, it Oh, well, okay, here's the answer. Ah, ah, ah, okay, this, this time around, um, we gave away 49 grantee— 49 grants. We're about to— the press release hasn't even gone out yet, so hot off the press. Uh, we are about to give out 49 grants worth $325,000. 6 in the Bronx, 19 in Brooklyn, 8 in Manhattan, 7 in Queens, 4 in Staten Island, 5 serve multi-burrows. 71% are serving environmental justice areas, and 80% are led by, uh, majority BIPOC leaders.
Okay, how many in Queens?

7. We've seen a slight decline in Queens, and we want to make sure that that goes back up. Now, I should point out though that there are some grantees that are multi-year grantees. So this is— these are new grants that are being made. So it doesn't mean that there are no other grants out there that are being spent. This is just the new money that we're about to distribute.
And you talked about potentially, uh, increasing in Queens. How, how would you go about that?

Any way that we can. It's really a matter of getting the word out. So, you know, we- we go to community boards, we— you know, all the same things that you've heard, all the methodologies, social media, email, community boards, in-person meetings, brochures, postcards, whatever we can do to get the word out. So we would love your help.

And I just want to add, I think the Green Fund Grant program, which is relatively new, is such a critical tool with helping these community-based organizations because as you know, they want and want to see a lot of activation of their parks, but they might not have the funds to do that. And so now the fact that they can go and get a grant to do an activity in their park for the community is just a really wonderful, um, kind of asset that we can provide these community groups.
Okay, thank you. Council Member Sanchez.

Thank you, Chair, um, and good afternoon. Uh, I'm on the same boat as

Council member Morano. We've been spending a lot of time today together, which is awesome. Um, so I, I first just wanted to start with just so much gratitude, uh, for the work that Partnership for Parks does, the support from the City Parks Foundation, um, and really, really, really give flowers to Pilar Maschi. I don't know if you know her, I mean, she's been there for a long time. Um, but just the work that she does to organize our friends groups in the West Bronx is transformational, right? It's, it's just incredible. Like, this woman will put up flyers. She'll just spend a whole day, like, putting up flyers on every building just to get folks out to a meeting and, and build that civic capacity. Um, and it's, it's really— it just really matters, right? Uh, we have very low civic capacity, er, ah, right now. Low civic engagement because we're such a low-income community. But this is what starts to transform that, right? Getting people involved. Um, so I have a very, uh, simple, direct question. Um, in preparation for this hearing, I reached out to all of my friends of parks groups at Aqueduct and at, uh, Washington's Walk and Sedgwick

and, and all the others. And I actually heard one thing resoundingly from them, which is a frustration around dealing with smoking in our parks. Um, just folks going in and they're smoking cigarettes, they're smoking marijuana, they're smoking, you know, around children and things like that. And so my question for you all is, um, you know, one, flagging it for you, uh, Matt, just to make sure, uh, it's on your radar for, for the PEP officers and every— and everything. But what should I tell our friends of parks volunteers regarding how, you know, they should best route those concerns because they're, they're concerned about, you know, getting into an altercation with folks like that.

Yeah, um, thank you, thank you, Council Member, for the question. That is a frustrating thing for the groups to have to experience. I really do recommend that groups use the 311 process. That would avoid that direct conflict, uh, with, with, uh, the person in violation of our park rules and that information does go to Park Enforcement Patrol. As you know, they might not be able to respond kind of in the immediate, uh,

timeframe, but having that record of complaints helps them, uh, figure out where they're doing regular patrol. So if we see a pattern of complaints coming in regarding smoking in a certain park, that will help them then, you know, try to send some resources there in the future. So I, I would, I would recommend that to the groups.
Thank you. And just to make this a hearing kind of— hearing style question, do you have information about how quickly you're able to respond to those kinds of requests?

Um, I don't have it here, but we could look at that data. Um, you know, because I think, you know, basically we would have the 311 data for complaints about smoking in parks, and we can show what the resolutions were. If I'm going to have to guess, most of them are going to be closed without being able to go right away, just just because of our, uh, enforcement capacity. But, you know, uh, you know, we can work with you on making sure the parks that people are complaining about, that we're getting— working with the captains there in the Bronx to have some patrols there.
Got it. And last follow-up, not advocating for this, just asking, does NYPD ever get involved, um, in this if a complaint is narrowly about smoking?

I think, you know, we work very closely with NYPD. They really focus on crime, um, and crime patterns, um, and I do not believe that they would— they do not really enforce against park rules in our parks.
Got it. And sorry, I said that was the last one, but this is the last one, I promise. Uh, what does a PEP officer do, uh, if they are able to make it in time?

Sure. I mean, I think that, um, for our PEP officers, um, you know, they are there to enforce park rules. Um, they would first to try to really educate the parkgoer. We try to use enforcement as a last resort, but they do have the ability to issue a summons, uh, for smoking in a park.
Okay, great. Thank you. Thank you so much, Chair.

I just want to go back, um, before, before we go to Harlem. I want to go

back to something you mentioned earlier about the data, um, the volunteer, uh, data that you have. Uh, is that compiled, uh, with the data that comes from NYC Service, or is it separate? Is it aggregated into one, or is it— is it—

Thank you for the question. So NYC Service's data is separate from ours. We compile and collect our own, uh, volunteer data and, uh, information. Um, each— we have multiple divisions, uh, within the Parks Department that collects the data. Um, and then we have a central repository for that information, um, called the Let's Green NYC initiative. And we store, um, the number of hours, the number of volunteers, um, that do formalized projects in our parks there. So the data from NYC Service though NYC Service may be involved in a project that we're doing, we collect the data ourselves through our different, um, management arms.

Thank you. Uh, what are the standards that DPR uses when a community group proposes youth programming, sports, wellness classes, cultural programming, um, to determine if such

programming will be allowed to occur on parks property?

Sure, thank you for the question. Um, you know, if a group is looking to do an event in our park, they would use the special event permit process to apply for- for such event. And, you know, we really do want to encourage groups to activate and use our parks, um, for those kind of variety of events, youth events, cultural events. We just need to screen them to make sure, you know, that where they wanna do the event is not already, you know, permitted for some other activity. We need to make sure, depending on the nature of the event, that they can provide the appropriate insurance. You know, if they need— as I stated before, if they need amplified sound, they have to get a sound permit. There are places that we don't necessarily allow sound. So, uh, that's what the role of our special event permit coordinators, um, are there to do, is to kind of take that application of what they're looking to do and help them work through and make sure they can run a safe, you know, event for the public. Again, we don't, um, do a lot of denials. I would say the main reason for denial is probably

going to be that the space is not available, um, because it's already permitted.

Sorry, I, I, I have a few groups in my district, um, that for some reason every summer they run into issues with the permitting office, I guess, particularly in Queens, um, to which either they're denied or they're just given a really, really, really hard time. Um, oftentimes our office has had to step in— well, the previous office has had to step in, um, and so that, that's why I asked the question, uh, what, what would constitute a denial? Because I do see it in my district quite often.

Um, you know, I'm surprised to hear that. I think we should work with your office to take a review of what you're seeing. We're happy to do that, um, because I think by and large, you know, we're, we're permitting like over 20,000 permits, you annually. Um, and so I think we are permitting a significant number of events in our parks and that, you know, in, in that process, you know, if this, the original site or the original day that somebody's looking to do, I think our permit coordinators really work with the applicant to try to find an alternate time or day to help them work to be

able to do their event. That is, that is what they do day in and day out. Um, so I'm, I'm surprised to hear of the difficulties. We certainly want to work with you to try to overcome them and have that be a smoother process.

I, I appreciate that. Uh, aside from conservancies that have formal contracts or licenses to perform maintenance activities in parks, do any volunteer groups or other local community groups perform similar maintenance activities or other park functions that, uh, DPR would otherwise perform?

Yeah, thank you, uh, Council Member, for the question. Um, so basically, as I said before, we have a huge maintenance staff that's on a schedule cleaning our parks, um, and we take great pride, um, in the level of cleanliness and care and condition that we keep our parks in. So, uh, you know, we do not see other groups coming in and, uh, you know, we step back while they step in. Uh, the volunteer work that's happening really is a supplement and an added value to the base level of care that we're providing for our parks.

Thank you. One final question and I'm going to turn over to Council Member Salaam. Uh, when a potential partner organization makes a proposal to parks but there are concerns about insurance, permits, staffing, safety, noise, lighting, or site conditions, who works with them to revise and fine-tune the idea?

So if, if a community-based organization is not affiliated with Partnership for Parks and they're just applying for a permit directly to the borough, the borough permit coordinator would work with them. But again, a plug for PFP here, um, you know, groups that are affiliated with PFP and have a community engagement coordinator, that person can really help them navigate the process and work with them to run a successful event.

Sorry, and I'll just interject quickly that if, if an event, a proposed event is of a specific size or scale, like typically over 500 or so, we actually have a dedicated citywide special events team for, for events that have a little more complexity or, you know, moving pieces a little more, hmm, you know, uh, substantial, for lack of a better word. Um, and that, then that team, similar to our

borough permit offices, can help applicants kind of, you know, uh, clarify policies and things of that nature as well.
Do the borough permit offices, uh, do they refer folks to, uh, PFP?

There's, there's essentially a— oh, sorry, yes, the permit offices are certainly, you know, our boroughs, our borough operations, our borough commissioners and their teams work very, very closely with PFP and our outreach coordinators. So, you know, we're one agency, one family. So, uh, yes, I think it's very common. I don't know if refer is quite the word, right word, but, you know, there's certainly dialogue, or it is not uncommon for, oh, hey, you know, we're interacting with this, uh, with this organization about a permit, but there's, you know, there's not a firewall that's not siloed. They'll have discussions with the borough commissioner, with our, you know, with the Partnerships for Parks Commissioner Smith, if you have anything else you want to add.

Um, sometimes the question may come in, like, if, if a group goes to the borough process and the borough will automatically ask, like,

are you affiliated with PFP? So the question comes up. If they're not, um, sometimes, yeah, again, referral may be not exactly the best word there, but, um, if they're not, PFP may be tagged and saying, like, you know, this group is coming to us often to do these things. You might want to consider working with them or something like that. So it comes in dribs and drabs in different ways.
Is it required that the staff person do that, or is it at their discretion?

Is it required— I'm sorry, you said, is it required— is it required that the staff person that's working with this group that's applying, um, and let's say this group is having issues, is it required that they, you know, uh, I don't want to use the, the term refer again, but I don't know what other term to use, refer them to PFP, or is it at their discretion to, to do so?

I, I, if I can, uh, I think I'd characterize for a permit— for a borough permit office, it may not be immediately clear that the applicant— you know, the applicant could just be an individual or a family, just, you know, right? Like,

it's not always immediately clear that they represent a formalized CBO or similar institute. So, uh, there's not really a formal mechanism in place for, again, a referral.
Do you think—

I think it's a more organic kind of process where —when we become aware of an organization and it becomes more substantial, that- that we wanna make sure they're aware of PFP and, and any resources that might be available to them.

Do you think it would be helpful if it was something that was required for them to say, if the- if there was a process in place? I'm asking because I, I, I never want it to be— well, I guess it— no one ever wants it to be that if there is a group that unfortunately, uh, has a bad reputation with the person they're working with at parks, that, you know, they may not have access to what other groups may have access to. Um, in term— do you get where I'm going with it?

I do and I think broadly speaking, I think we'd want to make sure that any, frankly, any individual, any group, any— whether formalized or not, we want to make sure if they want to help their,

their local parks and make those parks more exciting and better places to experience, we- we want to make sure they have access to that. And - and there shouldn't be any, uh, so to the degree that there is any, you know, sort of, uh, lesser-than treatment or anything like that. You know, if there is a relationship complication, some of these groups have known each other for years, or, you know, agency— if, if there's anything that needs to be resolved there, that's something we'd obviously want to know about and take a very close look at and do whatever we can to conflict resolution or whatever that might— path might be. Thankfully, it's exceedingly rare. Again, as Commissioner Nelson noted, you know, we are— tens of thousands of New Yorkers are coming to us every single day with things they want to do in our parks, whether that's through special event permits or or filming or athletic permits or what have you, or even outside of the permit process, interesting ideas, interesting proposals. And we do everything we can to, to hear those out and advance as many of them as possible, whether it's through formal permits or not. And that's, that's, that's something we want to continue, obviously, uh, er, ah, hmm, improving.
If, if various groups are having issues with, uh, a permit office, um, who would they escalate their complaint to?

So one of the, um, uh, er, improvements that we made when we took a look at the permit process is to really streamline and centralize the permit process. So in the past, borough permit offices, depending on the borough reported, had different reporting structures. So we streamlined it to have all the borough permit offices report directly to the borough commissioner in that, um, in that, uh, borough. Uh, so that's one change that we made. So you can escalate to the borough commissioner. Um, the other change we made is to really centralize policy. Um, so we have now a citywide, uh, special events policy office and a citywide, uh, athletic permit policy office. And so that also centralizes in making sure— we're trying to make sure that those standards and policies are, uh, uh, you know, kind of consistent across the boroughs, uh, and not just borough-based, for example.

You know, we- we make it, um, a point to, especially when we're dealing with

the police department, uh, to ask them about cultural training. Um, is that something that, that parks employees, particularly in the permit office, have to go through as part of their, their, their job responsibility, given that they're dealing with so many different community groups of different cultures uh, is that something they go through?

I, I, I think we have a high level of customer service and we do customer service training. Uh, we would have to check to see if that— like, what cultural components are included in that. I'm happy to get back to you on that.
How often is the customer service training, uh, uh, done?
I, I'll have to check and get back to you on that.
Okay, please. I, I would love the answer to those two questions. Thank you. Uh, Council Member Salaam.

Thank you, Chair. Uh, thank you for the testimony. DPR has approximately 85 contractual agreements with private organizations. Your private funding arrangements historically channel more resources towards parks in wealthier

neighborhoods. What is DPR's current framework for evaluating whether its CBOs and private partner agreements are equitably distributed across all 5 boroughs? And what metrics does the department use to ensure that parks in lower-income communities, which typically lack access to philanthropic support, are not falling further behind as the system increasingly relies on private dollars and volunteer labor?

Thank you, Council Member, for the question. Um, I think we— again, I think with the resources that we have as a city, um, do a great job at taking care of our park system with, you know, using city employees and city resources and capital dollars to renovate our parks. We do appreciate when private groups come in and can enhance the work we're doing with their private fundraising. But I recognize that, that is more easily able to do in certain neighborhoods than others. I think that, again, that's— it's why it's so important that we have this 30-year partnership with City Parks Foundation because they are out there fundraising from private donors to bring money into underserved parks. And through their Green Fund Grant program,

they're doing exactly that and bringing private dollars and allowing small community groups who may not have access to that fundraising resources themselves to apply for grants that they can then use to activate their parks and provide more programming and, um, activities in their parks. So again, I think this Partnership for Parks program that we're talking about is really one of the ways that- that Parks is working in this public-private partnership to bring more private dollars into under-resourced parks. Not only private dollars for their own activities, but it's funding, um, you know, it's funding the staff that are working with these communities to build capacity.
Definitely. We definitely need it.

I would, um, I would add a couple of things, um, when we started the Green Fund, it was really meant to be temporary. It was meant to help address funding cuts during COVID but what we found from philanthropists, frankly, was that the knowledge that we have of the community and the ability we have to vet projects and then distribute money made it possible for those funders to get money out into

neighborhoods that they, themselves would not necessarily make direct grants to. So we're definitely seeing that money being spread out in a way that it hadn't been before.
